result.summary: Pausanias describes Oropus, now Athenian, and the sanctuary of Amphiaraus near it. He covers the hero's deification, the five-part altar, the fountain and the dream-oracle ritual.

scenes.title: Oropus and Amphiaraus' fate
scenes.summary: Oropus passed from Boeotia to Athens. Amphiaraus is said to have been swallowed by the earth at Harma, and the Oropians first made him a god.

scenes.title: The temple and its altar
scenes.summary: Pausanias compares other deified men, then describes the statue and the altar's five divisions with the deities honoured on each.

scenes.title: Fountain and dream oracle
scenes.summary: The fountain receives coins from the healed. Pausanias explains Amphiaraus' dream divination and the ram-skin incubation rite.

alias_notes.explanation: Vesta is the Roman name of the hearth goddess, used by the translator.

notable_quotes.reason: Vividly describes incubation: sleeping in a ram's skin to receive a prophetic dream.

analysis.text: The passage shows how mortals could become gods through cult, and how Greek religion linked healing, oracles and ritual purity.
Oropus changed hands between Boeotia and Athens, and Philip of Macedon's grant reflects Macedonian power over Greek border disputes.

fun_facts.text: The Amphiareion at Oropos survives, with remains of its temple, altar and theatre.

language_notes.text: Philip is Philip II of Macedon, who defeated Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC and gave Oropus to Athens.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180-200 metres, so about 12 stades is a little over two kilometres.
Amphiaraus, a seer, fled from Thebes after the failed expedition of the Seven against it; Zeus opened the earth to save him.
Protesilaus was the first Greek killed at Troy; Trophonius was a hero with a famous oracle at Lebadea.
Alcmæon, son of Amphiaraus, killed his mother Eriphyle, who had betrayed his father for a necklace, so he is excluded from honour.
Lustrations are ritual purifications with water.
Hexameters are verses of six metrical feet, the usual form of epic and oracular verse.
This is incubation: sleeping in a sacred place so the god may send a healing or prophetic dream.

context_notes.text: Pæonian Apollo is Apollo as healer; Pæon was the physician of the gods.
Panacea and Hygiea were goddesses of healing and health, associated with Asclepius's cult.
Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus, was said to have founded an oracle at Mallus in Cilicia.

literary_notes.text: The hedge "they say" shows Pausanias reporting local tradition while keeping distance from it.
Pausanias defines Amphiaraus by his skill in dream divination, linking the hero's character to his later cult.
